title: Assessing the relationship between training load and injury in ultramarathon runners: a novel approach using Generalised Additive Models
authors: Burgess TL, Durand P, Buchholtz K
journal: South African Journal of Sports Medicine
population: 106 runners training for the 2018 Comrades ultramarathon; weekly data for 12 weeks before and 2 weeks after the race (retrospectively recalled)
findings: Injury incidence was 8 per 1,000 hours and the overall injury proportion was 40%; muscles (47%) and tendons (24%) were the most commonly injured structures, the knee (26%) and hip (19%) the most common sites.
Lower training distance in the 12 weeks leading to the race was linked to higher injury risk (p = 0.02), primarily occurring during or after the race.
Weekly training frequency had a significant heterogeneous (non-linear) relationship with injury risk (p = 0.02).
The ACWR effect on injury risk was minimal (p = 0.3); relationships between training load and injury were non-linear.
limitations: Retrospectively recalled weekly data in 106 runners at one race; injuries during or after the race are conflated with training injuries; low training load may mark pre-existing injury (reverse causation).
implications: Do not use ACWR as a hard injury-prevention gate: this study found minimal effect (p = 0.3), whereas [craddock-2020-acwr-two-oceans] (Two Oceans 56 km, n = 119) reported an injury association above ACWR 1.5. Keep ACWR as an informational display.
Flag a plan whose last-12-week distance is far below the athlete's own prior peak, since under-training was associated with more injury (direction only, no threshold).
Model load-to-risk non-linearly in any injury-risk estimator; avoid single linear thresholds.

verification.notes: Crossref (2025-07-09) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched; numbers confirmed. The researcher's description of Craddock 2020 as a Comrades cohort was wrong (it is a 119-runner Two Oceans study) and is corrected; Craddock is now its own entry.
